title: Ch. 5 Concept Drills
description: Generated concept drills for Chapter 5 (Unemployment and Inflation) written from the chapter learning objectives, because no Chapter 5 lecture slides were posted.

questions.prompt: The working-age population is 30,000 (thousand). 18,000 are employed and 1,200 are unemployed. What is the unemployment rate (two decimals)?
questions.explanation: Labour force = 18,000 + 1,200 = 19,200. Unemployment rate = 1,200 ÷ 19,200 × 100 = **6.25%**. (Dividing by the population, 4.0%, is the common trap.)

questions.prompt: Same data (population 30,000, employed 18,000, unemployed 1,200). What is the labour force participation rate?
questions.explanation: Participation rate = labour force ÷ working-age population = 19,200 ÷ 30,000 × 100 = **64%**.

questions.prompt: Same data. What is the employment–population ratio?
questions.explanation: Employed ÷ working-age population = 18,000 ÷ 30,000 × 100 = **60%**.

questions.prompt: Which of the following people is counted as unemployed in the Labour Force Survey?

options.text: A full-time student who is not looking for work.
A recent graduate with no job who applied to 20 employers last week and is ready to start work.
A parent who has left the workforce to care for a child.
A worker who stopped searching because he believes no jobs are available.

questions.explanation: To be **unemployed** one must be jobless, available and actively searching. The student, the caregiver and the discouraged worker are all **outside the labour force**.

questions.prompt: An unemployed person gives up looking for work and leaves the labour force. What happens to the unemployment rate, the participation rate and the employment–population ratio?

options.text: Unemployment rate falls, participation rate unchanged, employment–population ratio rises.
Unemployment rate rises, participation rate falls, employment–population ratio unchanged.
Unemployment rate falls, participation rate falls, employment–population ratio unchanged.
Unemployment rate falls, participation rate rises, employment–population ratio falls.

questions.explanation: The unemployed person leaves both numerator and denominator of the rate (rate falls) and the labour force (participation falls). Employed and population are unchanged, so **the ratio does not change**.

questions.prompt: The labour force is 20 million and 1 million are unemployed. If 500,000 of the unemployed stop searching, what is the new unemployment rate (two decimals)?
questions.explanation: New unemployed = 0.5 million; new labour force = 19.5 million. Rate = 0.5 ÷ 19.5 × 100 = **2.56%**, down from 5%, though no one found a job.

questions.prompt: A worker loses his job because the plant moved to a new technology and he does not have the skills required for the new jobs. This is…

options.text: Frictional unemployment.
Cyclical unemployment.
Seasonal unemployment.
Structural unemployment.

questions.explanation: A persistent **mismatch between skills and available jobs** is structural.

questions.prompt: A ski instructor is out of work each summer. This is…

options.text: Seasonal unemployment.
Cyclical unemployment.
Structural unemployment.
Frictional unemployment.

questions.explanation: Recurring, calendar-related joblessness (weather, tourism) is **seasonal**.

questions.prompt: During a recession many firms lay off workers because the demand for their products has fallen. This is…

options.text: Frictional unemployment.
Cyclical unemployment.
Structural unemployment.
Seasonal unemployment.

questions.explanation: Unemployment caused by a **downturn of the business cycle** is cyclical; it rises in recessions and falls in expansions.

questions.prompt: The unemployment rate is 7.5%, and the natural rate is 5.5%. How many percentage points of cyclical unemployment are there?
questions.explanation: Actual = natural + cyclical. Cyclical = 7.5 − 5.5 = **2.0 percentage points**. At full employment cyclical unemployment is 0.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the natural rate of unemployment is correct?

options.text: It equals cyclical plus seasonal unemployment and is zero at full employment.
It equals zero at full employment because everyone who wants a job has one.
It equals frictional plus structural unemployment, and the economy is at full employment when unemployment equals it.
It is the rate that occurs only during a recession.

questions.explanation: **Natural rate = frictional + structural** (also called the full-employment rate). It is positive.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would NOT be expected to raise the unemployment rate?

options.text: A longer period of Employment Insurance eligibility.
A binding increase in the minimum wage.
A rise in the share of workers covered by unions.
A job-search website that makes openings easy to find.

questions.explanation: EI extends search time, minimum wages above equilibrium and unions push wages above market, creating surplus labour. Better information reduces frictional unemployment.

questions.prompt: An efficiency wage is…

options.text: a wage above the market level that a firm pays to increase worker productivity.
a wage that the government sets as the legal minimum.
a wage negotiated by a union for all its members.
the market-clearing wage that equates labour supply and demand.

questions.explanation: Efficiency wages are **voluntary** premium wages. Reasons: lower turnover, less shirking, better applicants.

questions.prompt: Employment Insurance is likely to…

options.text: lower the unemployment rate and make recessions more severe.
raise the unemployment rate, but reduce the severity of recessions.
lower the unemployment rate and reduce the severity of recessions.
raise the unemployment rate and make recessions more severe.

questions.explanation: EI lengthens job search but supports the spending of unemployed households.

questions.prompt: The cost of the CPI basket is $400 in the base year and $450 in the current year. What is the CPI in the current year?
questions.explanation: CPI = cost of the basket in the current year ÷ cost in the base year × 100 = 450 ÷ 400 × 100 = **112.5**.

questions.prompt: The CPI was 140.0 in 2023 and 143.5 in 2024. What was the 2024 inflation rate (one decimal)?
The CPI tends to overstate the inflation rate. Which of the following is a reason?

options.text: The CPI is based on the prices producers receive, not what consumers pay.
The CPI ignores prices of services.
Consumers substitute away from goods whose prices rise, but the CPI keeps the basket fixed.
The CPI includes only imported goods.

questions.explanation: Biases: **substitution, new products, quality changes, outlet substitution**. Together they overstate inflation by about 0.5–1 percentage point.

questions.prompt: Which price measure includes the prices of imported goods that households buy?

options.text: The GDP deflator.
The PPI for domestic output only.
None of the three measures.
The CPI.

questions.explanation: The CPI follows what a typical household buys, whether made at home or abroad. The GDP deflator covers only goods and services **produced** in Canada.

questions.prompt: A worker earns a nominal wage of $30 per hour when the CPI is 120. What is the real wage in base-year dollars?
questions.explanation: Real wage = nominal ÷ CPI × 100 = 30 ÷ 120 × 100 = **$25**.

questions.prompt: Nominal GDP is $1,650 billion when the CPI is 110 (base year = 100). What is real GDP in base-year dollars (billions)?
Nominal incomes grow 5% and the CPI rises 3%. Real income grows by approximately…
questions.explanation: Real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation = 5 − 3 = **2%**.

questions.prompt: A loan has a nominal interest rate of 7% and the inflation rate is 2.5%. What is the real interest rate?
questions.explanation: Real = nominal − inflation = 7 − 2.5 = **4.5%**.

questions.prompt: Borrowers and lenders expected 3% inflation and agreed on a 5% nominal rate. Actual inflation was 5%. What was the real interest rate?

options.text: 2%, as expected.
0%, so the lender received a lower real return than the 2% expected.
−2%, so borrowers lost.
5%, the nominal rate.

questions.explanation: Ex post real rate = 5 − 5 = **0%**, versus the expected 5 − 3 = 2%. Unexpectedly high inflation helps borrowers and hurts lenders.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a cost of unanticipated (but not of anticipated) inflation?

options.text: Menu costs.
Paper money losing some of its value.
Arbitrary redistribution of income between borrowers and lenders.
The cost of reprinting catalogues.

questions.explanation: Menu costs and the erosion of cash holdings occur with **anticipated** inflation. Unanticipated inflation also causes redistribution and uncertainty.

questions.prompt: If the inflation rate falls from 5% to 3%, the price level is falling.
questions.explanation: Disinflation is a *slower* rate of inflation; with inflation still 3%, the price level is still rising. A falling price level is deflation.
